name: North America
title: The Atlantic Exodus
pitch: A refugee fleet founds a federation on the best rivers, coal and water power on Earth.

core.d: The Allegheny and Monongahela meet to form the Ohio, so boats reach the whole Mississippi basin from here. The Pittsburgh coal seam sticks out of the hill across the river, and iron ore, clay, limestone and timber are all within a few days.

start.n: Head of the Hudson tide (later Albany)
start.d: The fleet lands in April 1243 where ocean ships stop on the Hudson. Cohoes Falls and the Mohawk Valley route west are next door; the core moves to the Forks in years 6–10.

facts: ~300,000–1,000,000 across the Ohio Valley, Great Lakes and middle Mississippi (guess; estimates for all of North America run 2–18 million)
Humid continental: cold winters, hot humid summers. Pittsburgh today ~-2 °C in January, ~23 °C in July
~900–1,100 mm, spread through the year; spring floods on the Ohio
~150 frost-free days in upstate New York, ~170–180 at the Forks, ~200 at Cahokia
Iroquoian (New York, Ontario), Algonquian (Hudson, Great Lakes), Siouan (Oneota, probably Cahokia), others unknown
Native copper cold-hammered into ornaments; no smelting, no iron
Dogs only. No cattle, horses, sheep, pigs or chickens anywhere in the Americas north of the Andes
Maize (dominant since ~1000), squash, sunflower and native seed crops; beans spread across the Northeast only ~1300
No smallpox, measles or malaria yet; that is both the opportunity and the danger

land.d: Steep wooded hills cut by deep valleys, with coal, clay and sandstone in the hillsides. Narrow but rich bottomlands; no malaria.
A 1,580 km river from the Forks to Cairo, with wide terraces and floodplains. Spring floods can rise 10–15 m, so towns go on high terraces.
Flat glacial plains with deep fertile soils under oak-hickory and beech-maple forest, wet in spring. Later the Corn Belt.
Rolling limestone country with phosphate-rich soils, open woods and cane. Excellent for cattle and horses.

land.n: Lake Erie and Lake Ontario lowlands
land.d: Flat shore plains warmed by the lakes, good for orchards and grain. The Black Swamp west of Lake Erie is a huge wet forest.
The landing zone and the only low gap through the Appalachians to the Great Lakes (the later Erie Canal route). Fertile flats, long cold winters.
Long parallel ridges and narrow valleys east of the core, with poor ridge soils but rich limestone valleys. A barrier to the Atlantic coast.
The wide Mississippi floodplain opposite later St. Louis, home of Cahokia. Very fertile but flood-prone.
Tallgrass prairie with forest along the rivers and some of the deepest topsoil on Earth. Needs a steel plow to break the sod.
Pine and birch on the Canadian Shield, short summers (~110–140 frost-free days). Copper and iron country, too cold for reliable maize.

peoples.popText: ~10,000–15,000 in the center at its peak ~1050–1100; by the 1240s probably ~5,000–8,000 and falling (guess)
peoples.culture: Maize farmers ruled by hereditary chiefs from mound-top temples; Monks Mound is ~30 m high. Possibly Siouan-speaking. A stockade was built in the 1100s.
peoples.d: The biggest town north of Mexico, already past its peak. Gifts, food storage and vaccine could make it the federation's western anchor.

peoples.n: Lower Illinois Valley Mississippians (Spoon River, Dickson Mounds)
peoples.culture: Mississippian farmers mixing with local Late Woodland people, mounds and palisaded towns.
peoples.d: Fertile river valley on the way to the lead district. Face Oneota raiding from ~1300.

peoples.popText: ~2,000 at the town plus ~1,000 on farmsteads at its maximum (site overview)
peoples.culture: Mississippian chiefdom with 19 mounds on the lower Ohio; maize, fish and river trade.
peoples.d: Controls the lower Ohio near its mouth; a natural ally on the river route to Cahokia.

peoples.popText: A ceremonial center with few residents in 1100–1300; ~1,000 by 1400 (IUPUI research)
peoples.culture: Mississippian chiefdom on the Ohio near later Evansville, with a large platform mound and stockade.
peoples.d: Small now but growing; it will be the main Mississippian town on the middle Ohio.

peoples.n: Wickliffe and the Ohio-Mississippi junction towns
peoples.culture: Small Mississippian chiefdoms where the Ohio meets the Mississippi.
peoples.d: Gatekeepers of the river junction; the federation's boats pass right by them.

peoples.popText: ~5,000–15,000 in many towns around later Nashville (guess)
peoples.culture: Mississippian chiefdoms with stone-box graves and mound towns along the Cumberland.
peoples.d: Reachable by boat from the Ohio. Part of the southern Mississippian world, less tied to Cahokia.

peoples.n: Fort Ancient villages (Miami and Scioto valleys)
peoples.popText: Villages of ~100–500 people; perhaps ~10,000–30,000 in all (guess)
peoples.culture: Maize-bean-squash farmers in circular villages around a plaza, each village moving every 20–30 years (SunWatch near Dayton is the best known). Village councils, no great chiefs.
peoples.d: The core's nearest big farming population. Egalitarian villages that would trade for iron and oxen readily.

peoples.n: Fort Ancient villages (Kanawha and Big Sandy)
peoples.culture: Fort Ancient farmers and hunters in river-valley villages, using the Kanawha salt licks.
peoples.d: They sit on the Kanawha salt springs, so salt is the first deal.

peoples.popText: Stockaded villages of 50–100 houses (~200–500 people); perhaps ~5,000–15,000 in all (guess)
peoples.culture: Maize farmers in circular stockaded villages on ridge tops above the rivers, moving uphill after ~1250 because of raiding. Language unknown.
peoples.d: The people living at the core itself. Their land and goodwill come first; raids between villages mean a peace-maker is welcome.

peoples.n: Whittlesey people (Cuyahoga and Lake Erie shore)
peoples.culture: Farmers in villages on bluffs and promontories above the Lake Erie rivers, ~1000–1600.
peoples.d: Control the Lake Erie outlet of the core's north routes and Cuyahoga Falls.

peoples.culture: Iroquoian-speaking maize farmers in longhouse villages, organized by matrilineal clans with strong clan mothers. Ancestors of the Cayuga, Onondaga, Seneca and Oneida.
peoples.d: Closest big farming people to the landing and the Onondaga salt. Clan mothers control the fields, so ox-plows win them.

peoples.culture: Early Mohawk (Iroquoian) farming villages along the Mohawk River.
peoples.d: Right on the route west from the landing. The first neighbors, and the first test of the charter's 'no land taken' rule.

peoples.popText: ~15,000–30,000 in southern Ontario (guess); ~750 village sites known from later centuries
peoples.culture: Iroquoian farmers shifting to settled longhouse villages (Early-to-Middle Iroquoian, ~1300 change). Ancestors of the Wendat and Neutral.
peoples.d: Across Lake Erie and Lake Ontario; reachable by lake boat once the federation has them.

peoples.culture: Algonquian-speaking farmers, fishers and hunters in small villages under local sachems.
peoples.d: They live where the fleet lands. The first impression of the federation is made with them.

peoples.culture: Algonquian farmers and shellfish gatherers, matrilineal clans, small independent bands.
peoples.d: Own the river mouth and New York harbor that every return fleet passes.

peoples.n: Shenks Ferry and Clemson Island peoples (Susquehanna)
peoples.culture: Village farmers on the Susquehanna, language unknown.
peoples.d: Between the landing and the core on the overland route through Pennsylvania.

peoples.n: Late Woodland Michigan peoples (Odawa and Potawatomi ancestors)
peoples.culture: Algonquian speakers mixing maize gardens with fishing, hunting and wild rice; seasonal moves.
peoples.d: Middlemen on the lake route to the Lake Superior copper.

peoples.culture: Mobile bands living by fishing, hunting and wild rice; they still dig a little copper from ancient pits.
peoples.d: They know where the copper lies. Need guides and fair trade, not settlers.

peoples.culture: Siouan-speaking farmers and bison hunters on the prairie edge, ancestors of the Ho-Chunk and Ioway. Rising raiders from ~1300.
peoples.d: Will push into Illinois as Cahokia fades. The federation's main frontier diplomacy problem in the west.

peoples.culture: A stockaded Mississippian colony among local Late Woodland people.
peoples.d: Shows how far Cahokia reached, and that its reach is shrinking.

resources.qty: modern: ~34 billion short tons originally in place (USGS), in a seam usually 1.5–2.5 m thick over ~15,000 km²
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops in the hillside across the Monongahela from the Forks, at river level; dig with picks and float it downriver. Mined here from the 1760s.
resources.d: The best-placed coal on Earth for a starting industry. Fuel for smithing at first, then coke.

resources.qty: modern: the same Pittsburgh seam at ~2.5–3 m, the best coking coal in the US; tens of millions of tons a year were coked here in 1900
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops along the Youghiogheny valley; boats reach it on the Youghiogheny and Monongahela.
resources.d: Makes the strong coke a blast furnace needs. Phase 5 of the plan.

resources.qty: modern: thin carbonate (siderite) and limonite beds, ~30–40% iron; fed dozens of charcoal furnaces from the 1790s
resources.reach: 1230: ore nodules and beds exposed in stream banks and hillsides; pick it up or dig shallow pits.
resources.d: Enough to start a bloomery and then a charcoal blast furnace near the core.

resources.qty: modern: small (a few cm to 1 m layers), ~20–50% iron, renews itself in decades
resources.reach: 1230: lifted with shovels from swamps and lake edges across the glaciated north; the easiest ore of all.
resources.d: The first local iron, in years 3–5, before the hill ores are mined.

resources.qty: modern: ~4,700 km² of limonite and siderite ore with limestone and forest; 65 furnaces, ~105,000 t of pig iron in 1856
resources.reach: 1230: ore in shallow beds on the hillsides above the Ohio; reached by boat downriver from the core.
resources.d: The richest charcoal-iron district of the region, right on the Ohio.

resources.qty: modern: a widespread bed ~2–6 m thick, quarried for flux and lime
resources.reach: 1230: exposed in valley sides near the Beaver River; quarry with wedges and burn in a kiln.
resources.d: Flux for iron furnaces, mortar, and lime for fields.

resources.qty: modern: thick fireclays under the coal seams; East Liverpool became 'Pottery Capital of the World'
resources.reach: 1230: exposed with the coal in hillsides and along the Ohio banks.
resources.d: Bricks, firebrick for furnace linings, pottery and crucibles.

resources.qty: modern: brines from deep salt-bearing rock; ~3.2 million bushels (~80,000 t) in 1846
resources.reach: 1230: salt licks and springs at the riverside (the Great Buffalo Lick); boil brine in pans. Deeper wells come later.
resources.d: The nearest big salt to the core, by boat down the Ohio and up the Kanawha.

resources.qty: modern: brine from Salina Group rock salt; ~3 million bushels a year by 1841, the largest US salt district in the mid-1800s
resources.reach: 1230: springs bubble up around Onondaga Lake's south shore; boil or sun-dry the brine.
resources.d: The landing's first salt works (years 3–5), in Iroquoian land.

resources.qty: modern: weak sulphur-salt springs; small, frontier salt works only
resources.reach: 1230: open springs and licks near the Ohio; ice-age mammoth bones lie in the mud.
resources.d: A minor salt source on the Ohio, and a famous fossil site.

resources.qty: modern: the 1859 Drake well field; hundreds of millions of barrels from the Pennsylvania field
resources.reach: 1230: oil floats on the creek; skim it with blankets. Native people already used it as medicine.
resources.d: Lamp oil, lubricants and pitch long before drilling.

resources.qty: modern: a ridge ~13 km long of high-grade Vanport flint, worked for 10,000 years
resources.reach: 1230: open quarry pits already in use by local peoples.
resources.d: Gunflints, millstone dressing and trade goods; known to everyone in the region.

resources.qty: modern: a famous building stone and grindstone bed ~10–60 m thick
resources.reach: 1230: exposed in river gorges near Lake Erie.
resources.d: Grindstones and millstones, needed for every mill and tool shop.

resources.qty: modern: a ~20–27 m drop, ~300 m wide; the Mohawk averages ~170 m³/s (my estimate from USGS records) and floods at 2,500 m³/s+
resources.reach: 1230: free to use; a mill race on the bank needs no dam.
resources.d: The first sawmill and gristmill site, beside the landing.

resources.qty: modern: ~51 m drop, ~2,400 m³/s average; ~4–5 GW of hydropower today
resources.reach: 1230: a portage is needed around the falls; small mills on the banks are easy, the giant power waits for dynamos.
resources.d: One of the greatest power sites in the world, for the electric phase.

resources.qty: modern: three falls with ~80 m total drop; made Rochester the 'Flour City' in the 1830s
resources.reach: 1230: open riverbank sites, deep in Iroquoian country.
resources.d: A ready-made mill town on the lake route.

resources.qty: modern: a gorge dropping ~60 m over a few km
resources.reach: 1230: mill sites on open banks; a short portage from the Ohio basin to Lake Erie.
resources.d: The north link of the core, and later the Ohio-Erie canal route.

resources.qty: modern: rapids dropping ~8 m over ~3 km; the only obstacle on the whole Ohio
resources.reach: 1230: boats must unload and portage at low water; mills on the bank.
resources.d: A canal around it unlocks the river to the Mississippi.

resources.n: Allegheny white pine and hemlock forest
resources.qty: modern: old-growth white pine to ~50 m and 1.5 m thick; northern Pennsylvania supplied the world's largest lumber boom in the 1800s
resources.reach: 1230: untouched old growth; float logs down the Allegheny to the Forks.
resources.d: Masts, planks and ship timber.

resources.qty: modern: about a quarter of the eastern forest's trees were American chestnut before the 1900s blight
resources.reach: 1230: all around the core; endless charcoal and rot-proof chestnut and oak for building.
resources.d: Charcoal for iron, tannin for leather, and chestnuts as food.

resources.n: Deer, elk, turkey and passenger pigeons
resources.qty: modern: passenger pigeons numbered ~3–5 billion before extinction; deer and elk common (bison were rare east of the Mississippi in 1230)
resources.reach: 1230: hunted everywhere; pigeons can be netted by the thousand in migration.
resources.d: Meat and hides until the carried herds grow. No local animal can be milked or yoked.

resources.qty: modern: the most productive of the Great Lakes; sturgeon, whitefish, walleye and perch
resources.reach: 1230: shore seines and weirs at river mouths.
resources.d: Protein and fish oil a few days' walk north of the core.

resources.qty: modern: ~40 litres of sap make 1 litre of syrup
resources.reach: 1230: sugar maples in every northern forest; tap in March, boil in iron kettles.
resources.d: Sugar for rehydration salts, preserving and trade.

resources.qty: modern: ~4,000 km² of limestone grassland, later the world's horse-breeding capital
resources.reach: 1230: open woods and canebrakes reached by the Kentucky River.
resources.d: Where the carried horses and cattle should breed fastest.

resources.qty: modern: Mammoth Cave (~680 km of passages) and other caves supplied most US saltpeter in the War of 1812
resources.reach: 1230: leach the cave dirt with water and wood ash.
resources.d: Saltpeter for gunpowder, fertilizer and nitric acid.

nearby.qty: modern: ~5 million t (11 billion lb) mined 1840–1968; single masses up to tens of tons
nearby.reach: 1230: pure metal lying in veins and boulders at the surface; ancient pits already dug by Native miners.
nearby.d: Pure copper with no smelting needed. Wire for the telegraph comes from here.

nearby.qty: modern: small, never profitable for industry; thousands of ancient pits
nearby.reach: 1230: shallow pits on the island; only by canoe or boat across Lake Superior.
nearby.d: A summer mining camp, best for a story scene.

nearby.qty: modern: hundreds of millions of tons of high-grade hematite and magnetite since 1844
nearby.reach: 1230: rich ore cropping out in hills near Lake Superior; found in 1844 by a compass going wild.
nearby.d: The best iron ore in reach once lake ships carry it south.

nearby.qty: modern: billions of tons; the biggest iron range in the US, mined open-pit since 1890s
nearby.reach: 1230: soft ore just under thin glacial gravel, but far beyond the lakes' end.

nearby.qty: modern: ~860,000 t of lead and ~1.5 million t of zinc mined; ~27,000 t of lead ore in 1845
nearby.reach: 1230: galena crystals in shallow crevices, dug with picks; known to local peoples.
nearby.d: Lead for type metal, pipes, glass glazes and shot.

nearby.qty: modern: the Old Lead Belt plus a hill of almost pure hematite (Iron Mountain, Pilot Knob)
nearby.reach: 1230: iron ore boulders on the hill surface; a short walk from the Mississippi.
nearby.d: Iron near Cahokia for the western towns.

nearby.qty: modern: ~20 billion t originally; the world's largest anthracite field (~1,200 km²)
nearby.d: Smokeless coal near the landing route.

nearby.qty: modern: large magnetite bodies at Port Henry and Lyon Mountain, ~50–60% iron
nearby.reach: 1230: outcrops near Lake Champlain, upriver from the landing by boat and portage.
nearby.d: Iron for the Hudson settlements before the Forks.

nearby.qty: modern: high-grade brown ore that armed the Continental Army
nearby.reach: 1230: shallow ore beds near the surface, ~60 km east of the Hudson.
nearby.d: The closest good iron to the landing.

nearby.qty: modern: beds a few metres thick, mined since the 1840s
nearby.reach: 1230: exposed in the Grand River banks.
nearby.d: Land plaster for clover and plaster for building.

nearby.qty: modern: ~900 km² of oyster reef, once half the world's oysters
nearby.d: Food for the landing camp and lime from the shells.

nearby.qty: modern: tens of millions of beavers in North America before the fur trade (guess)
nearby.reach: 1230: beaver everywhere; trapped and traded by Algonquian bands.
nearby.d: Beaver fur is the main export through the gate.

nearby.qty: modern: once the richest cod ground on Earth (collapsed 1992)
nearby.reach: 1230: by ocean ship off Newfoundland; on the way home along the westerlies.
nearby.d: Salt cod for the return voyages.

nearby.qty: modern: ~750 km², volcanic soil, fresh water
nearby.reach: 1230: uninhabited and unknown to Europe until the 1420s.
nearby.d: The secret gate's waystation and quarantine island.

nearby.qty: modern: ~2–3 million t of tin produced over 4,000 years
nearby.reach: 1230: Europe's main tin source, bought through Pisa or Bristol traders.
nearby.d: Eastern North America has almost no tin, so bronze and solder rely on the gate.

nearby.qty: modern: about a third of all mercury ever mined
nearby.reach: 1230: in Castilian hands, sold through Mediterranean trade.
nearby.d: Mercury for thermometers, barometers and gilding.

nearby.reach: 1230: the merchant house partner; source of glass, books, dyes, alum and craftsmen.
nearby.d: The other end of the gate.

newcomers.num: ~1,500 in the first fleet; hundreds a year later (guess). Hungary lost ~15–50% of ~2 million people in 1241–42
newcomers.d: Plow farmers and cattle people with nothing to go back to. They fit the settler core well and the Native towns slowly.

newcomers.num: ~40,000–80,000 came into Hungary with Köten in 1239; a few hundred families could join (guess)
newcomers.d: Horse and sheep herders, enemies of the Hungarians since Köten was killed. Ideal for horse breeding and the prairie; need careful handling on the ships.
Forest farmers, carpenters and fur trappers, used to cold winters and river trade. Good woodsmen for the Ohio forests.
Farmers and miners from Silesia, which has silver and lead mines; useful mining skills.

newcomers.num: ~300–500 skilled workers in the first fleet (guess)
newcomers.d: Smiths, millwrights, masons, glassmakers, shipwrights and midwives. City people, so the forest and the Native towns are a shock.
Crews and builders for the fleet, from the coast where Béla IV hid. They become the federation's ocean pilots.
Starving families from England, Flanders and Germany, recruited through the gate. Farmers who know wheat and cattle.

newcomers.num: Village by village; tens of thousands over decades (guess)
newcomers.d: Farmers already; clan mothers adopt ox-plows and new seed. They keep their clans and send speakers to the council.

newcomers.n: Monongahela and Fort Ancient villages joining
newcomers.when: From ~1249, when the core moves to the Forks
newcomers.d: Village farmers right at the core who gain peace, iron and vaccines.
Chiefdoms used to big public works and stored food. They join as equals under their own chiefs.

neighbors.d: Powerful Mississippian chiefdom, rising as Cahokia falls. Rich in ritual copper and shell; trades with the Ohio Valley.
The second-biggest Mississippian center, at its height ~1200–1300 on the Black Warrior River. Hierarchical and organized.
A rich ritual center on the Arkansas River, trading as far as the Gulf and the Plains.
Cliff-dwelling farmers far to the southwest. The Great Drought (1276–99) empties the region; no contact for decades.
Divided city-states after Tula fell (~1150). The Aztecs found Tenochtitlan ~1325. Writing, calendars and markets, but no iron or ships.
Farmers and canoe people on the islands the fleet passes. Contact means disease risk both ways, so the fleet should avoid them.
Farmers who still sail to Markland (Labrador) for timber. Weak and fading; the Western Settlement is gone by ~1350. A small risk of word reaching Norway.
Arctic sea-mammal hunters moving from Alaska into Greenland in the 1200s. No threat, far north.

neighbors.n: Pisa and the Pisan merchant house
neighbors.d: The partner city. Loses to Genoa at Meloria in 1284, so the gate needs a backup.

neighbors.n: Frederick II (Holy Roman Empire and Sicily)
neighbors.pop: ~1–2 million in the Kingdom of Sicily (guess)
neighbors.d: The patron who knows the secret. Dies 1250; his dynasty falls by 1268.
Ruined by the Mongols, then rebuilding with stone castles. Béla's gratitude can send refugees willingly.
Batu's empire on the Volga, the cause of the refugee wave. It never reaches the Atlantic, but it reshapes eastern Europe for 200 years.
